meaning.text: In popular speech the word dolya is sometimes used in the sense of a positively happy fate, and with the negative ne (nedolya) in the sense of an unhappy, sorrowful fate.
Russian tradition personifies the fate bestowed upon a man at his birth as a supernatural being called Dolya.

appearance.text: She is described as a poorly dressed woman.
She is capable of transforming herself into various shapes.
In a Little-Russian tale, the rich brother's Dolya appears as a woman in beggar's rags.

scene.text: In a Little-Russian tale, the poor brother, hired to reap for his rich brother, meets the brother's Dolya in the harvest field walking among the shocks of grain.
In a variant tale of two fisherman brothers, the poor brother goes to the river at night and hears splashing as the rich brother's Dolya drives fish into his brother's net.

appearance.text: The Sreća is described as a beautiful girl.
As the evil Sreća (Nesreća) she is represented as an old woman with bloodshot eyes.

behavior_habitat.text: Machal calls the Sreća the Serbian counterpart of the Russian Dolya.
She bestows welfare upon the mortal to whom she is assigned, caring for his fields and grazing his flocks.
In national songs and traditions the Sreća frequently occurs as an independent being by the side of God.
The Sreća is not only good but also evil; as evil she is misfortune personified and may be called Nesreća.
The evil Sreća is always sleeping and takes no notice of her master's affairs, although she is also said to be engaged in spinning.
She usually lives behind the oven.
She is either good or evil.
The good Dolya protects her favourite by day and by night and serves him faithfully from his birth to his death.
The good Dolya takes care of his children, waters his fields and meadows with dew, and works for him.
The good Dolya drives fish into his nets and swarms of bees into his hives.
The good Dolya protects him against wild beasts and guards his flocks.
The good Dolya gets purchasers for his goods and increases the price of his crops.
The good Dolya selects good, full ears from other people's sheaves for him.
The good Dolya bestows good health upon him.
No one will succeed unless she helps him, and without her assistance all his efforts are in vain.
The man who gets an evil Dolya (Nedolya, Licho) finds all his toil of no avail.
The evil Dolya does nothing but sleep, dress herself or make merry, never thinking of offering him any aid.
Her power has no limits; a proverb says, "Not even your horse will get you away from your Dolya."
In a Little-Russian tale, the rich brother's Dolya pulls the largest ears from the sheaves the poor brother received as wages and sticks them into the sheaves of the rich brother.
In the same tale, the poor brother's Dolya is called a white-hands who thinks only of songs and finery, and so he is poor.
In the fisherman variant, the poor brother's Dolya is lazy and lies belly-up on a stone, singing songs and playing the gusli.
In popular songs the bitter, unkind Dolya is born together with a person, follows him step by step through his whole life, and sees him into the grave.
According to popular conviction, Dolya and Nedolya act by their own reckoning, independently of the will and intentions of the person they belong to.
When the Dolya leaves her client and stops working for him, he falls into poverty.
The activity of Nedolya is always directed to a person's harm: while she is awake misfortune follows misfortune, and it becomes easier only when she falls asleep.
Afanasyev holds that Dolya and Nedolya are living mythical persons, identical with the maidens of fate (rozhanitsy).

dealing_with_it.text: It is impossible to get rid of the Dolya: all attempts to sell her, make her lose herself in the woods, or drown her in the sea are bound to fail.
In the fisherman variant, the poor brother rushes to the stone and whips his lazy Dolya with a lash.
A bride going to her wedding addresses her Dolya in a song: if she is good, sit with me on the cart; if she is bad, float away with the water.
In a song the singer carts the bitter Dolya to market to sell her, but people know her and will not buy, so the singer throws her down from the cart.
In another song a girl bids her evil Dolya go and drown herself, or lose herself in the woods or perish in the field, and the Dolya answers that she will cling to her.
A saying advises: when Likho (Nedolya) sleeps, do not wake it.
Unlike the Dolya, a man may get rid of the evil Serbian Sreća (Nesreća) and drive her away.

origin.text: The Dolya is the fate bestowed upon a man at his birth, personified.
In popular songs the evil Dolya is born together with the person she follows.

rationale.text: Machal records the Dolya as Russian tradition.
Machal records the Sreća as the Serbian counterpart of the Russian Dolya.
Afanasyev independently prints Dolya and Nedolya tales, songs and sayings, including a Little-Russian tale and its Great-Russian version.

Machal's passage on the Dolya cites no source, so it is counted independent of Afanasyev, although the services of the good Dolya he lists closely follow those the Dolya names in Afanasyev's Little-Russian tale.
The Serbian evidence rests on Machal alone; Karadžić glosses Срећа only as the common word fortuna.

notes.text: names.primary.native: the only form tied to a listed people is Machal's romanised Dolya ("Russian tradition ... called Dolya", machal1918:p.251), recorded as a Latn row. Afanasyev prints the Cyrillic Доля (afanasyev1869:p.392, p.404) and Недоля (p.403, p.404), but only inside a Little-Russian tale (малорусская, p.392), a Great-Russian tale (Великорусская редакція, p.393) or general popular belief (p.396, p.404) with no listed people named, so no Cyrillic row was written. Searched доля, недоля, dolya, nedolya in all sources.

Unmapped people terms: 'малорусская' (Little-Russian, afanasyev1869:p.392) and 'малороссійскихъ' (Little-Russian songs, afanasyev1869:p.394), proposed Ukrainians; the table lists Малороссія and Little-Russians but not these Russian adjectives. 'Великорусская' (Great-Russian, afanasyev1869:p.393), proposed Russians. Clauses from these pages keep the source word and no people row was written for them.

Top-level fields hold the Dolya as Machal (Russian tradition) and Afanasyev (Little-Russian and Great-Russian tales and songs) describe her; the Serbian Sreća, which Machal calls her counterpart and describes differently, is kept as the serbian-sreca variant. Karadžić s.v. Срећа glosses only the common word (das Glück, fortuna); it is cited only for the printed native form.

Unread pages in the Afanasyev chapter: afanasyev1869:pp.398-402 (continuation of the songs on Беда, Горе and Лихо that p.396 says replace Nedolya; may hold more Nedolya material) and afanasyev1869:p.411 (find hit: 'недоля также прядет нити', Nedolya also spins threads, in the Serbian usud/sreća section pp.409-411). ralston1873:p.197 footnote glosses dolya as 'lot, share' and was not opened. Not read to keep within budget.

related: Machal gives Licho as another name for the evil Dolya (machal1918:p.252), and Afanasyev uses Likho for Nedolya in a saying (afanasyev1869:p.404); recorded as 'related' rather than a stronger relation.
